# Introduction

## From Chatbots to Agentic Engineering

### What changes when AI systems can use tools and work across multiple steps

A chatbot usually responds to one request at a time: you ask, it answers, and
you decide what to do next. An agentic workflow extends that interaction into a
loop. Given a goal, an AI system can break the work into steps, use tools, check
the results, and decide what to do next. A coding agent, for example, might
inspect a repository, change a file, run its tests, and use the test results to
guide another change.

The important distinction is not that an agent is a model with human-like
independence. The model proposes actions, while the surrounding software
determines which actions are available, how they are carried out, and whether
the system can continue without approval. Connecting a model to tools can make
it more useful, but it also means that mistakes can have consequences beyond a
poor answer.

Agentic systems therefore need boundaries as well as capabilities. Useful
designs make actions visible, limit access to what the task requires, define
when a person must approve consequential steps, and provide a way to stop or
recover from a failure. The goal is not autonomy for its own sake; it is
reliable work that people can understand and control.

### The agentic engineering stack: models, harnesses, tools, memory, and governance

Building such systems means working with more than a model. The **model**
interprets input and proposes responses or actions. A **harness** supplies the
runtime loop that calls the model, manages the task, and decides how to handle
its proposed actions. **Tools** connect that loop to services and information,
while an **execution environment** determines where code or other operations
run and what they can access.

Longer-running work may also need **memory and state** so the system can retain
relevant information between steps or sessions. **Orchestration** coordinates
steps, tools, or multiple agents. **Governance and observability**—including
permissions, approval points, logs, and evaluation—help people understand and
constrain the system's behavior. These layers can overlap in a particular
product, but separating them is a useful way to reason about how a system is
built and where to improve it.

This is the book's practical point of departure: choose and connect components
to fit a real task, then make the resulting workflow dependable and
controllable. The chapters that follow examine these layers in turn, from
models and local inference to harnesses and complete working stacks.

:toolbox: _The Book of Agentic AI — A practical guide to understanding agents and building a practical toolkit._

The Book of AI is an attempt to be a practical guide to understanding agents and building an AI toolkit you control. It is a living document, and the landscape is changing rapidly. The book is structured to provide both a high-level overview and practical guidance for building and using agentic AI systems.

This book focuses on [{{< glossary "Agentic Engineer" popup="hover" >}}](https://davidgeeraerts.github.io/AI/appendices/glossary.html#agentic-engineer) — the disciplined practice of designing, orchestrating, and governing systems of AI agents that plan, act, observe, and iterate — and on the [{{< glossary "Agentic engineering stack" popup="hover" >}}](https://davidgeeraerts.github.io/AI/appendices/glossary.html#agentic-engineering-stack): the layered set of models, harnesses, tools, memory, orchestration, and governance required to make those agents reliable and controllable in real work.

Use this book as a living toolkit: consult the chapters for practical
orientation, and follow the linked source materials and quarterly snapshots as
the landscape changes.
